sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Seonangshin** ​(*seonangshin*) — ‌Village Guardian, ‌Boundary · ​Village spirit ​— ​belongs to ​the Korean ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Village ​Guardian, Boundary". ‌The name ​means ‌"Village spirit"[^1].

​**Seonangshin** is ​the village ​guardian spirit ​who ​protects settlements, ‌boundaries, and ​travellers from ‌harm ​in Korean ‌tradition. The ​name means ‌"Village spirit" ​and ‌belongs to ​the domain ​"Village Guardian, ‌Boundary." Seonangshin ‌is ‌the spirit ​who guards ​the village ‌boundary, usually ​honoured ​at a ‌shrine near ​the entrance ​to the ‌settlement. ​The deity ‌is believed ​to protect ​the community ​from ​epidemics, disasters, ‌war, and ‌wandering malevolent ​forces.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as **Seonangshin** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/seonangshin/). ​The restoration ‌needs no ​distinctive letters ​or ​diacritics its ‌ASCII form ​would lose, ​which ​places the ‌name in ​Tier 2. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *seonangshin* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Hangul ​+ Hanja ​as **서낭신 ​(城隍神)**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Village ‌spirit"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form *seonangshin* ‌survives only ​because ‌the early ​domain-name system ‌could ​not carry ​diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Seonangshin** recovers ​the full ‌diacritic ​detail of ‌the scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ‌the address ‌bar. The ‌restoration ​needs no ​distinctive letters ‌or ​diacritics its ​ASCII form ‌would ​lose, which ​places the ‌name ​in Tier ‌2.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **s** ​→ ‌**S** — ‌Same, capitalized
​- ‌**e** → ​**e** — ​Same
- ‌**o** ‌→ **o** ‌— Same
‌- ​**n** → ‌**n** — ​Same
​- **a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**n** → ​**n** ‌— Same
​- **g** ​→ ​**g** — ‌Same
- ​**s** ‌→ **s** ​— Same
‌- **h** ​→ ‌**h** — ‌Same
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ​— Same
​- ‌**n** → ‌**n** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/sʌ.naŋ.ʃin/** — ​Korean ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **sʌ** ‌— ​The first ​syllable of ‌Seonangshin, carrying ​primary stress ‌in ​the romanised ‌form.
- ​**naŋ** — ​The middle ​syllable ​or element, ​pronounced with ‌level pitch ​in ‌Korean.
- ​**ʃin** — ‌The final ​syllable, often ‌closing ​in a ‌nasal or ​simple vowel ​in ‌the Korean ‌reading.

For ‌the modern ​speaker, the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​'suh-NAHNG-sheen' — ​The first ‌vowel is ​a ​mid back ‌unrounded vowel; ​the second ‌syllable ​contains a ​velar nasal. ​The name ​is the ‌Korean ‌reading of ​the Sino-Korean ‌term for ​a city-moat ​guardian ‌deity.

Kindred ‌and historical ‌forms of ‌the ​name:

- ‌**Hangul** — ​서낭신 — ​the Korean ​script ‌form.
- ​**Hanja** — ​城隍神 — ​the ‌Sino-Korean character ​form.

The ​first vowel ​is a ‌mid ​back unrounded ‌vowel; the ​second syllable ‌contains a ​velar ‌nasal. The ‌name is ​the Korean ​reading ​of the ​Sino-Korean term ‌for a ‌city-moat guardian ​deity.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved ‌in ​Hangul + ​Hanja ​as **서낭신 ​(城隍神)** ​— ‌Korean alphabet ​+ ​Chinese characters, ‌attested ​Modern Korean, ‌in ​Korea. ‌The script ​is ​written left-to-right.[^1]

​The ​scholarly ​transliteration is ‌*Seonangsin* ​(Revised Romanization), ‌giving ​the ‌normalized reading ​/sʌ.naŋ.ɕin/.

‌The rendering ​proceeds ‌step ​by step:

​- ‌Hangul 서낭신 ‌with ‌Hanja 城隍神 ​— ​the ‌village guardian

​Korean ​names may ‌be ​written ​in Hangul, ‌the ​indigenous Korean ‌alphabet, ​and ​sometimes in ​Hanja, ​the Sino-Korean ‌character ‌set. ​For **Seonangshin**, ‌the ​Hangul form ​is ‌**서낭신** and ‌the ‌Hanja ‌form is ​**城隍神**. ‌Hangul ‘서낭신’ ​and ​Hanja ​‘城隍神’ (Seonghwangsin ‌in ​Sino-Korean reading); ​the ​figure ‌is also ​called ​Dongbaek Seonang ​or ‌Dodangsin ​in regional ‌cults. ​The ASCII ‌form ​*seonangshin* is ‌a ‌technological ​compromise; the ​capitalised ​restoration **Seonangshin** ​is ‌the ‌scholarly citation ​form.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Seonangshin** ​is ‌the village ‌guardian ​spirit ​who protects ​settlements, ​boundaries, ​and travellers ‌from ​harm ​in Korean ‌tradition. ​The ‌name means ​"Village ‌spirit" ​and belongs ​to ​the ​domain "Village ​Guardian, ‌Boundary." ​Seonangshin is ‌the ​spirit ‌who guards ​the ‌village ​boundary, usually ‌honoured ​at ​a shrine ‌near ‌the ‌entrance to ​the ​settlement. ‌The deity ​is ​believed ‌to protect ​the ​community ‌from epidemics, ​disasters, ‌war, ​and wandering ​malevolent ​forces.[^1]

​### Village ‌Guardian

‌Seonangshin ​defends the ‌settlement ​and ​its people ‌from ‌harm.

‌### Boundary ‌Shrine

​The ‌seonangdang marks ​the ​threshold ​between civilised ‌space ​and ​the wild.

​### ‌War ​and Protection

​The ​spirit ‌is invoked ​against ‌invasion, ​epidemic, and ‌disaster.

​### ‌Community Rites

‌Annual ​dongje ​festivals renew ​the ​bond ‌between village ‌and ​guardian.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​mythology of ‌Seonangshin is ‌preserved in ​Korean oral ​tradition, shamanic ​ritual texts, ​and classical ​sources such ‌as the ​Samguk Yusa. ​The narratives ‌are not ​merely stories; ‌they encode ​social ‌values, ritual ​obligations, and ​relationships between ​humans, nature, ​and the ​sacred. Some ‌details vary ​by region ‌and by ​shamanic lineage.[^1]

‌### The ​Shrine at ‌the Village ​Gate ‌(Village cult)

​Every traditional ​village had ‌a seonangdang, ‌a small ‌shrine at ​the boundary ​where the ‌village met ​the wilderness. ​Offerings of ‌rice wine, ​cloth, and ​prayers were ‌made ​there to ‌keep disease ​and disaster ​outside the ​community.[^2]

### ​Guardian of ‌the Threshold ‌(Boundary myth)

​Seonangshin was ‌imagined as ​a warrior ​or official ‌who patrolled ‌the margins ‌of ‌settlement. People ​passing through ‌the boundary ​bowed or ​left a ​small offering ‌to ensure ​safe travel ​and to ​avoid offending ‌the guardian.

​### The ​Dongje Festival ​(Communal ‌rite)

Village ​communal rites ‌(dongje) gathered ​the entire ‌community at ​the seonangdang. ‌The rite ‌renewed the ​covenant between ​the village ​and its ​guardian, strengthening ‌social solidarity ‌and collective ​protection.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Seonangshin ​sits ‌at ‌the ​intersection of ​indigenous ​Korean ​village ​guardian ‌cults ​and ​the ‌Sino-Korean ​city-god tradition. ‌Confucian ​reformers ‌promoted ​official ​worship ​of ​local ​tutelary ‌deities, while ​shamanic ‌practice ​preserved ‌the ​older ‌spirit ​cults ‌at ​village boundaries. ​The ‌figure ‌also ‌overlaps ​with ​military ‌hero ​cults: ​generals who ‌defended ​a ​region ‌were ​sometimes ‌posthumously ​honoured ​as seonangshin. ​Today ​the ‌seonangdang ‌survives ​as ‌a ​heritage ​site, ‌and the ‌rites ‌are ‌sometimes ​revived ‌as ​community ​festivals ​rather ‌than as ​explicit ​religious ​worship.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures ​in ​the ‌PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ‌include ​[[andvari|Andvari]], ‌[[cerberus|Kérberos]], ​[[fafnir|Fáfnir]], ‌[[garmr|Garmr]], ‌[[goshin|Goshin]], ​and ​[[medousa|Médousa]], ​each linked ​through ‌guardian ‌/ ​protector.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus is ‌yet ​assigned ​to ‌Seonangshin ​with certainty. ‌That ​absence ‌should ​be ​read honestly: ​for ​a ​Korean ‌name ​of this ‌type ​the ‌material ​record ‌is expected ​to ‌be ​thin, ​and ‌the ‌primary evidence ‌remains ​the ​textual ‌testimony ​gathered in ​the ‌Scholarly ​Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were such ​evidence ‌to ​surface, ​it ​would take ​recognizable ‌forms: ‌votive ​or ‌dedicatory inscriptions ​naming ​서낭신 ‌(城隍神), ‌sanctuary ‌or ‌cult remains ​tied ‌to ​village ​guardian ​and iconography ‌matching ​its ​traditional ​attributes ‌(seonangdang shrine ​and ​geumjul ​sacred ‌rope). ​Each candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed ​against ‌the reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.
